# Defang version drift review

Verdict: BENIGN for SHA-256 e446ae23382c2a28072c59761e54b09d0ab27480ddf9b1725e48c48f3bd673bc, the Go proxy source ZIP for DefangLabs/defang v3.15.5-0.20260918121944-508333ae2026+incompatible.

## Decisive comparison and execution paths

Forager recovered the original v3.15.4+incompatible Go module ZIP and its provenance. Both archives contain the same 72 members. Only `.github/workflows/go.yml` differs: the smoke-test timeout rises from 45 to 90 minutes, and workflow dispatch is retried twice if a competing run cancels it. Run identification uses `display_title` instead of `name`. There is no change to the install workflow, npm source, package scripts, or any other shipped member. Today's scanner flags the same installer primitive in the earlier release too; the queue's earlier clean result is not reproducible with this rule set.

The installation workflow evaluates `curl -fsSL s.defang.io/install`, checks `defang --version`, repeats for a pinned version, and invokes `bash <(curl ...) nightly`. The installer recovered at commit 508333ae2026 is byte-identical to v3.15.4 (SHA-256 e0da944d3fa6687fbdaea740f8ed610ec48a98f5484d16c2ab7f4f46c05e1cba). It queries the project's GitHub releases, optionally authenticating to that API with GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN to avoid rate limits. OS and architecture select a release asset. It downloads and extracts that asset, moves `defang` into the configured install directory (default ~/.local/bin), sets execute permission, offers PATH and completion configuration, runs `defang completion`, and removes the temporary archive and extraction directory. These are disclosed installation effects; the self-referential eval command in the installer's header is a usage comment, not self-execution.

The npm entrypoint imports `run()`. That function checks the installed CLI version or GitHub's latest release, validates the version string, constructs the platform asset name, downloads through s.defang.io, writes the archive, extracts the named executable, sets permissions for ZIP contents, removes the archive, and calls `spawnSync(pathToExec, args)` with inherited stdio and environment. Arguments remain an argv array. No package-install lifecycle hook runs this path. The MCP JSON configurations select `defang mcp serve`. The Base64 README deeplink decodes to the same MCP launcher configuration; it is not an executable concealed stage.

The randomized sleep in go.yml follows a failed Git push, fetch, and rebase during the vendorHash repair job. Its 1-5 second delay avoids competing pushes. Neither this sleep nor a tar extraction in ordinary build logic establishes C2, anti-analysis, or SSH transfer.

The mutable main.tar.gz and installer URLs were recovered separately with provenance. The current installer differs from the pinned installer only in comparing shell basenames before installing completions twice. The current Windows redirect selects v3.15.8, and Go buildinfo identifies github.com/DefangLabs/defang/src/cmd/cli with cloud SDK dependencies. These current bytes are not asserted to be the submitted release's original binary. Source startup calls command.SetupCommands/Execute and flushes telemetry. Telemetry sends an anonymous ID, event, properties, OS and architecture through the project's client and honors DEFANG_DISABLE_ANALYTICS. There is no evidence here of substituted assets, credential theft, or an unauthorized execution surface. The actual deployment and historical mutable URL responses are unavailable.

## Rule corrections and retained coverage

The cases.json id_map records all relocated observations. Matcher and scope preservation applies to both randomized-sleep observations, tar xzf text, and curl command-substitution text. The sleep rules remain notable; unsupported C2/anti-analysis mappings were removed. Local tar text now lives with archive extraction and no longer supplies bare SSH context. `scp-tar-sync` still requires SCP and references the moved atom. Curl stdout capture belongs with curl client behavior, not a claim that a file was saved; its response-acquisition and Lazarus consumers reference the new ID.

Curl-to-eval moves from a C2/dropper objective to a notable script-evaluation deployment capability. The old raw regex also matched comments, printed examples, and curlish command names. The replacement matches a parsed eval call whose argument begins with a curl substitution. Its existing exclusions remain intact. Plain eval no longer supplies the legacy suspicious fetch-eval grouping; the plugin consumer references the relocated atom explicitly. The only other ancestor consumers of the moved objective atoms are PE-only CrystalX/hosts-sinkhole rules, whose scopes never included these shell/workflow observations.

The existing shell process-substitution atom now examines an actual command node and accepts curl's scheme-less URLs. It still recognizes HTTPS use, excludes output substitution, and does not treat documentation comments or printed examples as executed shell commands. Its two pacman consumers retain the same ID. The existing registry-hook-propagation.sh fixture retains both hostile propagation detections and its three suspicious observations.

`python3 testdata/taxonomy/shell-curl-eval/check.py` checks 19 positive, near-miss, both-claim, and consumer controls plus that existing propagation fixture. Controls include C2 polling and padded-delay composites to verify retained objective coverage. A bounded search of other supplied text samples and small ZIP members found no additional instance of the original eval-curl regex outside this package. Existing shell fixtures and all exact/ancestor consumers were inspected before changing the shared rules. No attack-specific matcher was deleted to clear a verdict.

## Reproducible scan results

Local slow scans with reference following disabled were used to compare identical input bytes. The original ZIP changes from 0 hostile / 1 suspicious / 207 notable to 0 hostile / 0 suspicious / 209 notable. Both embedded eval run bodies retain the notable deployment observation; the nightly run gains process-substitution coverage. The current main archive changes from 0 hostile / 1 suspicious / 605 notable to 0 hostile / 0 suspicious / 607 notable; the usage comment ceases to establish eval execution. No accurate operation is lost. The five retired IDs are replaced by their neutral IDs, and the existing process-substitution observation gains a supported match.

The model's probability for the original ZIP changes from 0.92299783 to 0.9169582. Its calibrated level remains -1 and alert confidence remains 0 before and after. The main archive changes from 0.76796126 to 0.7385841, likewise without a calibrated alert. High raw probabilities alone do not establish malicious behavior. The source analyzer reports some embedded-source and interprocedural-flow limitations; execution paths above were read directly rather than inferred from missing findings.

The current Windows ZIP baseline has 0 hostile / 0 suspicious / 269 notable observations (the PE member has 260 notable observations). Native Rizin recovery reached its 600-second limit and the PE report explicitly records `disassembly-incomplete`; `cleave facts` recovered imports and Go module identity but no function/call graph. Go objdump also could not recover runtime.pclntab. Consequently this review does not claim complete native execution coverage or a reconstructed build. No changed rule targets PE bytes.

The repeated Windows scan retains exactly the same trait IDs and levels: 0 hostile / 0 suspicious / 269 notable for the ZIP, including 260 notable for defang.exe. Its probability remains 0.6462196, with calibrated level -1. Both scans carry the native disassembly limitation, so this is retained partial static coverage, not a complete native execution proof.
